ADMINISTRATIVE SERVICES:
 
a. Consideration of award of Contract B23-09-029 for the Broadband Equity,
Access, and Deployment Program (BEAD) Challenge to High Street
Consulting Group, LLC and to authorize change order authority to the County
Manager for 10% of the contract amount, and authorize the County Manager
to execute the necessary documents :
Grant Evans stated that the BEAD program is a new program, a one-time
appropriation for broadband expansion and that it was created by the current
administration in infrastructure to serve the unserved and underserved
properties, businesses, and residents across the country.  He talked about
the definition of unserved and underserved as defined by the FCC and
indicated that the areas that have been identified as unserved or
underserved are eligible for the funding.  He stated that each state will
oversee their own funding which is overseen at the federal level by NTIA,
that as part of the process each state is required to administer a challenge
process and that the process is only open to local governments, nonprofits
and internet providers to review the data and challenge, where necessary, to
add in properties that should be eligible for the BEAD funding that are not
currently identified.  Mr. Evans indicated that the ACA is overseeing the
program for Arizona, that last October they issued their guidance for how the
program will work and that around that time Navajo County formed a BEAD
Task Force to capitalize on the middle mile construction program and the
BEAD funds.  He stated that the Task Force is recommending that a
consultant be hired for the BEAD Challenge Process.  He indicated that the
goal of this contract is to assure that all properties in Navajo County are
identified and accounted for except for the Reservation properties, due to not
having the authority or jurisdiction to carry out the challenge process on the
reservation so that will have to be led by the tribal authorities.  Mr. Evans
spoke about the process and timeline, indicating that it will start March 1
  
                                                                    3 of 11 
DRAFT

<!-- page 12 -->
through April.  He stated that they are asking for approval today so that the
consultant can get started with gathering and analyzing data, as well as
doing a public awareness campaign so that citizens can be aware and be
active participants.  Mr. Evans talked about the partnerships, stating that the
Task Force consists of all of the cities and towns within Navajo County and
NPC and that they have all verbally agreed to a financial commitment, as
well as from APS and SRP. He thanked Rochelle Lacapa for her assistance
through the collaborations and relationships she has. He talked about a
Utilities Grant Program, for communities affected by the coal plant closures,
that Ken Maruyama has submitted for, indicating that they anticipate to
received twenty-five-thousand dollars from that.  He stated that they have
approximately $105,000 total in anticipated partner and grant contributions
for this project. He talked about working with the Task Force and partners to
discuss additional funding.  He talked about the RFQ process, indicating that
they received seven proposals, and that High Street Consulting Group was
the highest scoring respondent.  He stated that staff is recommending
approval.   
Supervisor Whitesinger inquired approximately how many people this will
serve?
Mr. Evans stated that they have approximately twenty thousand addresses
that they will be targeting and talked about the importance of the community
outreach to make sure that the properties do speed tests or provide
documentation that they are not offered the services that are reported.
Supervisor Seymore thanked Mr. Evans for his work and for gathering all
the partnerships for this project.
Supervisor Whitesinger thanked Mr. Evans, Ms. Lacapa and all those that
have helped with this project. She talked about how we sometimes take
broadband for granted when we have it available but indicated that there are
those who don’t have the accessibility and may need it for education,
medical or other purposes.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to approve award of Contract
B23-09-029 for the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment Program
(BEAD) Challenge to High Street Consulting Group, LLC and to authorize
change order authority to the County Manager for 10% of the contract
amount and authorize the County Manager to execute the necessary
documents, motion seconded by Supervisor Seymore. Vote unanimous
approving the motion.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to enter into the Navajo County
Public Health Services District Board of Directors Session, motion seconded
by Vice-Chairwoman Benally.  Vote unanimous approving the motion.

1. Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number
02-2024 adopting the Hearing Officer Rules of Procedure for Animal Care &
Control and Environmental Health :
Rhonda Krouse discussed the item indicating, that in the past they have no
other option but to rewrite citations for animal violations and notice of
violations to establishments for repeat offenses, which utilizes their
resources and makes it were they are unable to respond to more animal
calls and complete more inspections.  She stated that with the approval of
this Resolution for civil violations, it will decrease many of the repeated calls
and they will be able to focus on responding to more calls.  She further
stated that other departments can also utilize the services of the hearing
officer.   
Chairman Whiting thanked Ms. Krouse and her team for working on this,
indicating that many citizens have asked for help, that in the past we haven’t
had a solution but that this will help provide a way to move forward.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
02-2024 adopting the Hearing Officer Rules of Procedure for Animal Care &
Control and Environmental Health, motion seconded by Vice-Chairwoman
Benally.  Vote unanimous approving the motion. 
 
  
2. Presentation to inform on most recent Fatality Review data:
A presentation was shown.  Alyssa Lemmon stated that she has been
coordinating the county fatality reviews for the past four years, stating that
the fatality reviews are conducted because many deaths and preventable. 
She talked about the process that they use for the fatality review, indicating
that from the nineteen child deaths in Navajo County, sixty-three percent
could have been prevented.  She talked about the recommendations for
prevention, indicating that they found four main categories where actions
  
                                                                    5 of 11 
DRAFT

<!-- page 14 -->
could be taken to prevent death, including pregnancy strategies, parenting
strategies, school and community involvement and general service
utilization.  She indicated that many of the recommendations in the
categories are considered education focused, that at the Health District they
have several programs providing education services identified in the reviews
and talked about some of the different services including mental health for
both adults and youth.  She talked about overdose deaths, indicating that
they reviewed twenty-nine of the fifty-three deaths from 2021, that they are
not reviewing the deaths that occur on tribal land or where tribal land is
listed as the primary residence due to difficulties in receiving records from
tribal entities on child deaths and the program being minimally staffed.  She
talked about some of the common factors in overdose fatalities, including
incarceration history, adverse childhood experience and use of more than
one substance and the recommendations including, improved support,
enhanced training for first responders, improve care coordination until
release from incarceration and establishing emergency department
discharge protocols and education.  She talked about services offered
through the Health District including free Narcan/education, established
community hotline and certified staff for Peer Support Specialists and ACE
trainers. She stated for the Suicide Mortality, they did eighteen of forty-three
reviews, indicating that for the same reasons mentioned previously they did
not review tribal deaths.  She talked about common factors, including
adverse childhood experience, some form of crisis within two weeks of the
death, suicidal feelings, thoughts, intentions or plans within a month of the
death, signs/symptoms of behavioral health challenges or alcohol
consumption prior to death.  She further talked about the recommendations
including increased access to mental health services, crisis response
teams, improved support for childhood traumas, social connection,
improved training for healthcare and criminal justice staff.  She talked about
services offered by the Health District, including certified staff as mental
health first aid and ACE trainers, mental health first aid and ACE classes,
free gun locks and a veterans resource guide. She talked about barriers that
have been identified to the review process and community concerns.  She
reviewed ways that people can provide support, indicating people can
participate with the community health improvement plan workgroups and
listen to those with lived experiences and in recovery.  She stated that the
annual Fatality Review Reports can be found on the county website. 
           
Supervisor Seymore indicated that the data is great information, indicating
that unless you know where you’re at you don’t know where to make
improvements.  He talked about the Reaching Rural program bringing things
before the Board that can help.  He talked about how he reached out to the
schools to be able to share information to help break some of the barriers
through education. He thanked Ms. Lemmons and her team for the work
they have done on this.    
Supervisor Whiting shared his appreciation for the presentation and the
hard work they have done.  He spoke about the importance of being aware
of this topic.  He indicated that it is not always that people are unwilling but
that there are a lot of misconceptions and that hopefully we can have the
hard conversations and look for solutions moving forward.

seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote unanimous approving the

PUBLIC WORKS:
 
PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT: 
 
1. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 03-2024, approving/denying a Special Use Permit to allow for the
construction of a 105’ monopole communication tower and associated
facilities located north of the Winslow area:
Tyler Richards stated that this is for a cellphone tower north of Winslow.  He
talked about the location for the proposed tower and indicated that it is
zoned A General.  He reviewed the site plan, indicating that it will be a
one-hundred-five-foot tower, that the setbacks are in excess of the
ordinance requirements, that they are planning on having a twelve-foot
access road for emergency vehicles, there will be a ten-foot fence
surrounding the facility and that the equipment will sit on a five-foot
platform.   He stated that the applicant did hold a community meeting, but
that there was nobody in attendance at the meeting.  He reviewed the staff
analysis, indicating that it has been properly noticed and posted, that it
complies with the Zoning Ordinance and meets several of the goals of the
Comprehensive Plan, that it has been determined to be compatible with
current and likely future uses and that there are no minimal adverse effects
on public health.  He stated that staff has not received any public comments
either in favor or against the project.  He further stated that staff is
recommending approval and that the Planning and Zoning Commission
unanimously recommended approval at their December 14, 2023, meeting,
subject to the conditions provided.   
The applicant (appearing virtual) did not wish to speak.
 
Chairman Whiting opened the public hearing, there being no comments,
the public hearing was closed.
 
Supervisor Seymore talked about the requirements for the tower height
having been eight-foot and one-hundred-foot and requested clarification
regarding the proposed tower being recommended for
one-hundred-five-feet.   
Mr. Richards stated that the maximum height requirement for a
non-residentially zoned tower can go up to one-hundred-ninety-nine-feet.   
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
03-2024, approving a Special Use Permit to allow for the construction of a
105’ monopole communication tower and associated facilities located north
of the Winslow area, motion seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote
unanimous approving the motion.
 
  
2. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution

2. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 04-2024, approving/denying text amendment to Article 15, Section
1502 and Article 30, Section 3002 regarding swap meets:
Sondra Starkey stated that this proposed text amendment for swap meets is
due to several code enforcement concerns as well as inquiries from the
general public.  She stated that this amendment would be to include a
definition for swap meets, indicating that in their research they found several
jurisdictions include auctions as well, and that this would be to have in in the
zoning ordinance as a permanent use for a property.  She stated that in the
staff report she attached track changes for Article 15 and 30 showing the
definitions and usages.  She stated that staff, as well as the Planning and
Zoning Commission, recommend approval.       
 
Chairman Whiting opened the public hearing, there being no comments,
the public hearing was closed.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
04-2024, approving text amendment to Article 15, Section 1502 and Article
30, Section 3002 regarding swap meets, motion seconded by Supervisor
Seymore.  Vote unanimous approving the motion.
 
  
3. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 05-2024, approving/denying text amendment to Article 25, Section
2503, regarding accessory building setbacks, and Article 25, Section 2520,
regarding accessory dwelling units:
Sondra Starkey stated that this is for a text amendment after finding a
couple of discrepancies between code enforcement inquiries, as well as
inquiries from the public. She stated that the first amendment they are
proposing is to update the three-foot accessory building setback to a
five-foot setback, which falls in line with fire code.  She stated that the
second amendment they are proposing is that zoning districts, which
currently allow for accessory dwellings, to also allow for park models as
guest houses, which will comply with recent changes to the statute.  She
indicated that the third amendment they are proposing is the removal of the
remaining reference to servant’s quarters, stating that it was resolved in a
previous amendment that updated it to guest houses instead of caretaker’s
quarters.  She stated that staff, as well as the Planning and Zoning
Commission, recommend approval.    
 
Chairman Whiting opened the public hearing, there being no comments,
the public hearing was closed.
 
Supervisor Seymore requested clarification on if a modular unit or park
model in a site-built subdivision could be added as a second home.  
Ms. Starkey stated that it would be dependent on the master development
plan and the CCNR’s that were established at the time. She provided some
different examples.  She stated that it would still need to be under seventy
percent of the square footage of the primary home, since that is a
requirement for secondary dwellings or guest houses. 
Supervisor Seymore inquired if a permit would be required.
Ms. Starkey stated that it would be required not only a guest house permit,
  
                                                                    8 of 11 
DRAFT

<!-- page 17 -->
but also a building permit. 
Supervisor Seymore talked about keeping the neighbors looking nice and
not allowing them to become downgraded by allowing park models to come
into areas where everything has been site built.
Ms. Starke stated that it doesn’t change the developments were guest
houses wouldn’t be allowed that it just in the zoning districts where they are
already allowed.   
 
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
05-2024, approving text amendment to Article 25, Section 2503, regarding
accessory building setbacks, and Article 25, Section 2520, regarding
accessory dwelling units, motion seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger. 
Vote unanimous approving the motion.
 
4. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 06-2024, approving/denying text amendment to Article 25, Section
2517 of the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance, regarding age of mobile
homes which require rehabilitation verification:
Sondra Starkey stated that this text amendment, indicating that last year
Planning had put through a zoning ordinance update that required a
twenty-year rolling basis for rehabilitation certification for manufactured and
mobile homes twenty-years or older and that this would be an update to
that.  She indicated that, in working with HUD, they do not require a
rehabilitation certification that extends past 1976, so they are requesting the
text amendment to reflect that any type of verification that the county would
need to go through the building department.  She stated staff is
recommending approval. 
 
Chairman Whiting opened the public hearing, there being no comments,
the public hearing was closed.
 
Supervisor Seymore discussed the item regarding older homes and stated
that he appreciates the work that staff has done on this.  
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
06-2024, approving text amendment to Article 25, Section 2517 of the
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance, regarding age of mobile homes which
require rehabilitation verification, motion seconded by Supervisor
Whitesinger.  Vote unanimous approving the motion.
 
  
COUNTY BUSINESS UPDATE: Report from County Manager, County Attorney
and Board members :
Bryan Layton reported that he and his family moved to Snowflake area and are
getting established there. 
Supervisor Seymore reported on the Legislative meetings, stating that he
appreciates the work of staff and CSA. He talked about the NACAO Executive
Meeting, stating that a two-million-dollar renovation of the Family Dollar in Taylor
has been approved to become the new Head Start and that it will be a great
addition to the community.  He further talked about how well the Head Start
program does in Navajo County, stating that there are openings in the program. 
He thanked staff for the great job with plowing snow to help keep things moving for
                                                                    9 of 11

the citizens.  He spoke of the possible changes to the budget, indicating that they
are proposing to keep local control. He stated that he is looking forward to 2024.   
Supervisor Peshlakai reported on attending Indian Tribes and Nations Legislative
Day, indicating that he was also able to meet with Representatives. He talked
about the meeting with the Army Corp of Engineers yesterday for a site visit at the
Winslow Levee. He thanked staff and spoke of the funding that we are receiving.
He stated that he has been attending the regular Chapters meetings and indicated
that he is looking forward to the one-on-one informational sessions with the
communities that he will be holding at the end of February. He spoke about
providing a comprehensive update to the Hopi Tribal Council at one of their
upcoming meetings.
Supervisor Whitesinger reported on meeting with Chris Pasterz to discuss
partnerships to develop industry within the communities, indicating that she is
grateful for all of our partners who are looking at ways to bring economic
development to our region.  She shared her appreciation to Representative
Peshlakai for the invitation to sit with her on the Legislative Floor on opening day.
She spoke about the Governors State of the State Address, noting that her
discussion really spoke about native Arizonians and serving Arizona. She listed
some of the things that were discussed.  She thanked staff for helping keep them
educated so they are able to advocate for our rural communities. She spoke
meeting with the Eleando family to talk about the impact that the newspaper article
had on them regarding their daughter who plays volleyball and was picked up by
Eastern Arizona College.  She talked about the importance of putting a spotlight on
our community members for some of the wonderful things that they are achieving.
Vice-Chairwoman Benally reported on the Indian Tribes and Nations Legislative
Day activities and the meetings that she had with Representatives to discuss
projects for District One and encourage them to continue to support the Winslow
Levee funding.  She spoke about the community workshops that Chris Pasterz did
in November for three of her communities. She thanked Mr. Pasterz and indicated
that one of the communities has applied for a grant for coal facilities, and that all of
her chapters will be given the same opportunity. She shared her appreciation to
Evelena Claw for assisting with road projects in District I and for her
communication with NDOT. She also thanked Nicole Reske for completing some
resolutions for the School Bus Route Study. She talked about the issues that they
have been having with the roads due to the flooding, snow, and mud, indicating
that they need help with the roads. She thanked NDOT and BIA for their assistance
with clearing the roads.  She talked about the need for gravel on the roads to help
stabilize them.   
Chairman Whiting thanked everyone for their outreach to the delegation at the
Capital, stating that they had great attendance at the CSA Legislative Reception,
where they were able to share different priorities and needs that the counties have.
He provided an update on Real AZ, indicating that it continues to be a productive
meeting and that they are seeing growth, not only in attendance but from different
communities and businesses that are meaningfully engaged.  He shared his
appreciation to Rochelle Lacapa for her role there and now Chris Pasterz,
indicating that the communities have shared the value that he is providing them
and how much they enjoy being able to collaborate and work with him.  He spoke
about NRWG, indicating that he believes this is quite a productive meeting for
Forestry issues and that he appreciates how the group collaborates and finds ways
to help each other.  He talked about the ECO committee, indicating that it continues
to be a productive tool and resource for our county.  He spoke about the Ranch

Motion before the Board:
Certificate of Removal and Abatement Purging Record of Tax, Penalty and Interest on Personal Property
Taxes, pursuant to A.R.S. §42-19118 and §42-18353
Background:
Pursuant to ARS 42-19118 the personal property taxes assessed against the property (Tax ID: 940016901,
029429001, 990000301, and 130000501) were determined to be uncollectible after a diligent search by
the Navajo County Sheriff's Office for various reasons. Personal property was removed from future tax
rolls by the Navajo County Assessor's Office. 
Pursuant to ARS 42-19118 the personal property taxes assessed against the property (Tax
ID 1400017601, 040065601 & 180017301) are uncollectible. After diligent search conducted by
the Navajo County Sheriff's Office for various reasons (Resided outside of Navajo County or plates
were obtained through MVD). Personal property has been removed from future tax rolls by the Navajo
County Assessor's Office.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. g.        
Meeting Date: 02/27/2024  
Title: Amendment No. 4, Employee Benefits Consultant B20-01-007
Submitted For: Eric Scott, HR Director  Submitted By: Cheryl Hollins, Account Specialist
Department: Administrative Services
Motion before the Board:
Amendment Number 4 extending Employee Benefits Consultant Contract No. B20-01-007 with The
Mahoney Group for one additional year from April 1, 2024, through March 31, 2025
Background:
On March 27, 2020, the Board of Supervisors approved the Contract with The Mahoney Group for
Employee Benefits Consultant, Contract No. B20-01-007. This contract has worked well for Navajo
County. This contract may be renewed up to four additional one-year terms. This would be the fourth
renewal and both parties are in concurrence. Staff recommends that the contract be extended for one
additional year from April 1, 2024, through March 31, 2025.

Meeting Date: 02/27/2024  
Title: Cancel and Appoint DWID
Submitted By: Rayleen Richards, Elections Director
Department: Elections
Motion before the Board:
Adoption of Resolution Number 07-2024 canceling the March 12, 2024, Election for the Timberland
Acres Domestic Water Improvement District and appointing the candidates pursuant to
A.R.S. §48-1012(E)
Background:
48-1012. Election of trustees; vacancies
E. If only one person files or no person files a nominating petition for election to fill a position on the
board of directors of the district, the county board of supervisors, by resolution, may cancel the election
for that office and appoint the person who filed the nominating petition to fill that position. If no person
files a nominating petition for an election to fill a district board office, the county board of supervisors,
by resolution, may cancel the election for those offices and those offices are deemed vacant and shall be
filled as otherwise provided by law. A person who is appointed pursuant to this section is fully vested
with the powers and duties of the office as if elected to that office.

Title: ARRF Funds request
Submitted By: Maxine Tyler, Executive Assistant
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
Approve a request from Darrin Reed Foundation for Attorney Anti-Racketeering Revolving Funds to
assist in the Darrin Reed Foundation Fundraising Dinner in the amount of $1375.00
Background:
The Darrin Reed Foundation, Inc., provides assistance in the community through law enforcement
officers.  Officers come across people that are in need of some help and are not able to pay for it out of
pocket.  The foundation also helps with training and equipment the agencies can't pay for but will benefit
law enforcement in fighting illegal drug trafficking.  At Christmas, the Foundation was also able to help
community members in need during the holiday season.  Twenty deserving families recommended by law
enforcement benefited from these funds.

$1000
Background:
Musical productions require rehearsals and a schedule.  The choir members and other students are
involved in every facet of the musical production.  This structure can help students and reduce the
opportunity for students to engage in behaviors such as drug use.  They form friendships with others that
have similar interests.  Participating in these events boosts self-esteem and confidence.  Students that
have a positive outlook towards themselves are less likely to succumb to peer pressure and drugs.

across such Road.

appurtenant components (collectively “Cables”) for the Project adjacent to, along, above, under or 
across such Roads.

and

Title: FY24 Arizona's Governor's Office of Youth, Faith and Family STOP Grant
Submitted By: Lynda Young, Office Manager
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
FY24 Governor's Office of Youth, Faith and Family STOP Grant #GR-STOP-GOYFF-010124-13
Background:
Arizona Governor's STOP Grant pays for the Navajo County Sexual Assault Response Team Coordinator
supporting victims of sexual assault. The purpose of a Sexual Assault Response Team (SART) is to
provide a coordinated and compassionate response to incidents of sexual assault.  This financial support
will allow us to provide support and enhance services for Sex Crime Victims in Navajo County.  We
utilize STOP funding to manage our local Navajo County Sexual Assault Response Team.

Executive Summary (500 word limit)
The Navajo County Sexual Assault Response Team improves communication and facilitation for a coordinated response to sexual assault within the 
county, from the first call through post-conviction to support the well-being of survivors and aim to bring responsible person(s) to justice.
Need – Sexual assault deeply affects communities nationwide, causing enduring harm to victims' physical, emotional, and psychological well-being. 
We have identified four areas of need for our victims of sexual assault:  1 – SART members need training resources for new members or existing 
ones. 2 – Less than 5% of sexual assault victims’ cases that come through the FAC are adjudicated.  Victims need closure through the justice 
system to increase resilience. 3 – Navajo County has no human trafficking data.  We know the victims are there, we aren’t tracking them.  4 - 
Navajo County’s citizens need to know of resources to victims of sexual assault. 
Target Population - Navajo County, located in northeastern Arizona, encompasses Show Low, Pinetop-Lakeside, Snowflake, Taylor, Holbrook, 
Winslow, and the unincorporated Heber-Overgaard community. It consists of over 50% Indian land, home to Navajo, Hopi, and Apache tribes. 
Demographically, it’s 42.9% white, 43.5% Native American, 12% Hispanic, with other races minimally represented, including African American, 
Asian, Native Hawaiian, and miscellaneous races.  Our gender demographics are 49.8% are female, with 50.2% male. Approximately 66% of 
Navajo County’s 9,949 sq. miles are Indian reservations. Despite its vast size, Navajo County is impoverished, with a 25.6% poverty rate, double 
the national average.
Program Strategy/Approach – Our program will consist of four primary functions that will directly impact the four identified problems.  With funds 
from this grant, will deploy the following strategies/approaches:  1) The SART coordinator will create an On-Boarding virtual and accessible training 
curriculum for local SART members and victim service providers. 2) We will examine local data and identify approaches to increase sex crime 
conviction rates.  We will collect data from cases, both referred by law enforcement and non-reporting adult victims.  We’ll develop an evaluation tool 
to examine each case’s unique circumstances.  3) We will gather data in year one, tracking Human Trafficking victims’ situations closely.  We will 
adapt and utilize the data and practices of the Arizona Governor’s Arizona Human Trafficking Council to assist us.  4) Our outreach plan is both 
community and agency specific.  We will booth regularly, meet staff at these agencies, and promote SART- specific services. In addition, our SART 
Coordinator will booth at various events around Navajo County and the State to engage communities with our program information.
Objectives and Performance Measures – We will monitor/measure this program as follows: Monthly review of SART cases to identify gaps and/or 
protocol/processes, victim surveys will measure the quality of services received, outreach activities will be tracked by number held, trainings will be 
tracked by number held, we will organize a community-wide awareness campaign for January, Human Trafficking Awareness Month, and Sexual 
Assault Awareness Month in April for each grant calendar year.  In addition, our SART Coordinator will booth at various events around Navajo 
County.  
Needs/Resources (1,500 word limit)
NEEDS AND RESOURCES
Problem
1. Sexual assault deeply affects communities nationwide, causing enduring harm to victims' physical, emotional, and psychological well-being.  70%
suffer severe distress, surpassing other crimes.  94% of women develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) , and 33% consider suicide .
Physical consequences include injuries, STIs, and unwanted pregnancies. It shatters one's sense of safety and control, often leading to drug use .
Their relationships with family, friends, and co-workers suffer.
2. In the United States there are approximately 463,634  victims of sexual assault 12 years of age (YOA) and older annually. In Navajo County, an
average of 100 individuals (60 primary victims, 40 secondary) aged 11+ seek help for sex offenses.   Navajo County, rural and impoverished, relies
on limited resources. Partnering and resource coordination are vital for comprehensive trauma-informed support. Our SART, initiated in 2018, is the
nucleus of this operation.  With funds from this FY23/24 grant, we will continue to maintain and enhance our SART, focusing on continued training
and outreach for law enforcement and create an On-Boarding Training Program available to all partner agencies, specifically new SART members.
To facilitate this training, we will need supplies for folders to be handed out with law enforcement and SART training.  In addition, we need a
projector screen and projector along with an Owl carrying case, to house the owl camera for our MDTs and trainings.  Our SART coordinator needs
a new laptop w/docking station, printer, along with printer ink.  In order to bring back education and training to the SART, we will send our SART
coordinator to one in-state 3-day training, and two one-day in-state training.  In addition, we’ll send the SART coordinator and the Victim Service
Manager to a National Sexual Assault Conference.  Information gleaned at these trainings will be shared with the SART and victim service
advocates.
3. Navajo County sees 60 sex crime victims, aged 11+, on average, but fewer than 20% reach the County Attorney's Office .  Less than 5% of
defendants are adjudicated, and only the same percentage of victims have their voices heard in court. Achieving closure through the justice system
is vital for healing and resilience. Our plan: Year one, gather case flow data; year two, identify red flags and service gaps, and make case flow
recommendations; year three, implement and assess these changes for improved conviction rates.
4. Navajo County lacks data on sex trafficking victims, a significant underserved group. With FY23/24 grant funds we will boost our SART to

Strategies/Approaches (1,500 word limit)
Strategies and Approaches
Our Strategies - Our program will consist of four primary functions that will contribute to sustainability and expansion of our Sexual Assault  
Response Team: 1) SART Team Management and Enhancement, 2) Increasing resilience in victims specifically by increasing cases referred to  
prosecution, 3) Providing services to an underserved population of victims of human trafficking.  4) Expansive Community Outreach.  To meet our  
goals and objectives, we will provide a dedicated and coordinated response to sexual assault victims 11 years of age and older within Navajo  
County. Our SART Coordinator is responsible for managing our SART and maintaining SART protocols, policies and procedures. To provide a  
consistent response to sexual assault victims, comprehensive interagency training is critical. Our SART Coordinator will coordinate and provide this  
training to victim service providers. As is common in most communities, the general public is not aware of the resources available should there be a  
sexual assault. Our SART Coordinator will conduct 10 outreach activities that will bring this information and education to the general public. 
1) SART Team Management and Enhancement: SARTs reduce the impact of trauma by activating interdisciplinary expertise to measure and  
address victims' needs. The collaborative partnerships formed by SARTs help reduce trauma, inform victims of available resources, and improve  
service accessibility for diverse populations. Our SART Coordinator will continue to manage our SART Program. SART members will refer and  
review sexual assault cases, discuss, and evaluate our effectiveness and develop ways to improve interagency responses based on victim-identified
needs and evidence-based practices. The SART coordinator will ensure the safety and confidentiality of our victims, manage protocol compliance,  
and update protocol as the need is identified. They will follow legislative changes that effect the investigation and services provided in our sex crime  
cases. The SART coordinator will track cases and obtain local and State data to identify service gaps. In addition to data tracking, the SART and  
Victims of Sexual Assault will be surveyed annually to evaluate the SART’s success. The coordinator will maintain partnerships between agencies 
while also performing outreach to agencies who are not currently members of SART but who would benefit the team. The coordinator will schedule,  
manage, and facilitate monthly SART team meetings.  In FY24, funds from this grant will assist the SART coordinator in creating an On-Boarding  
virtual and accessible training curriculum  for local SART members and victim service providers. This program will enhance the SART for FY24.
2) Increasing Resilience in Victims:  The trauma from sexual violence may impact a survivor’s employment in terms of time off from work, diminished  
performance, job loss, or inability to work. These issues disrupt earning power and have a long-term effect on the economic well-being of survivors  
and their families. Coping and completing everyday tasks after victimization can be challenging. Survivors may have difficulty maintaining personal  
relationships, returning to work or school, and regaining a sense of normalcy. With funds from this grant, we intend to increase resilience in sexual  
assault victims that have reported offenses, and the crimes were investigated.  Our goal is to examine local data and identify approaches to increase
sex crime conviction rates.  In year one of our grant, we will collect date from cases, both referred by law enforcement and non-reporting adult  
victims.  Develop an evaluation tool to examine each case’s unique circumstances including, victim and defendant demographics and lifestyle, their  
access to resources, law enforcement or other interventions and resources, and tracking the situations overall outcome.  By collecting and  
categorizing this data, we believe that by year two, we will be able to access/identify trends and provide recommendations of protocol/process  
change. Finally, by year three, we will roll out protocol/process and train members of the SART or any other agencies identified through this  
process.  Justice is critical to the wellbeing and safety of a victim and the community.  A successful prosecution of a sexual assault case facilitates  
healing and helps the victim overcome the trauma of sexual assault.  Each victory, each focused effort to get these cases through a successful  
prosecution, increases the victim’s resilience.  This increased resilience will combat the daunting need to re-enter their lives to work or school,  
connect with others, and regain some sense of normalcy.
3) Providing services to an underserved population of victims of human trafficking:  Currently, Navajo County Attorney’s Office has no data to  
analyze.  We have had a few cases resulting in a human trafficking arrest.  With a focus to identify this underserved population of victims of human  
trafficking, we will use monies from this FY23/24 grant to gather data in year one, tracking these victims’ situations closely.  Training and educating  
our ourselves, our partners, and local community on Human Trafficking and the unique challenges these victims face. We will adapt and utilize the  
data and practices of the Arizona Governor’s Arizona Human Trafficking Council to assist us in starting from our beginning.  In year two, we’ll  
assess/identify trends and provide recommendations and in year three, we will implement protocol/policy change and training. 
4) Community Outreach: Building relationships with people and organizations within our community is essential to the success of our SART. Our  
outreach plan is both community and agency specific. Not only does outreach educate the community about sexual assault and human trafficking,  
but it also provides critical information to the public aimed to reduce sex crime/trafficking incidents from occurring and assist victims through their  
recovery. A community educated about sexual violence is better able to support victims in need. An informed community can help reduce the shame

engage communities with our program information.
Our program has experience training and applied experience working with diverse groups of victims, including various ethnic groups including tribal  
communities, impoverished and under-educated, victims suffering from disabilities, and the LGBQT community.  Our victim advocates are the driver  
and enforcers of our SART’s practices and protocol.  They will be on the front lines working directly with our victims, advocating for victims, with the  
direction from our SART Coordinator.  They will be a victim’s primary point of contact for victims of reported and non-reported cases, and work with  
a victim for however long the victim is in need, even up to years in certain situations.  Our advocates are trained in cultural diversity with an  
emphasis toward the American Indian population which makes up the majority of our county’s population, trauma informed care, LGBQT  
communities with an emphasis toward the Indian population.  They receive on-going training and have extensive experience and can connect with  
individuals and tailor their approach and communication to support and assist each victim's unique needs. This experience has equipped them with  
the cultural competence and communication skills necessary to address the distinct challenges and barriers that different communities may face  
when dealing with victimization.

Collaborative Elements and Partners (1,500 word limit)
Navajo County, one of Arizona's smallest counties, relies heavily on inter-agency collaboration to deliver essential services. Our limited resources  
and absence of duplicative services make these partnerships vital. Our partner agencies include therapy services and two local shelters. These  
relationships have deepened over the years, strengthening our collective efforts.
Partnerships - Our SART has representation from the following core agencies: Law Enforcement, Mental Health Services, Medical Services, Victims  
Services, and Prosecution. The Navajo County SART program currently has a MOU with 11 partner agencies, working together to provide a  
collaborative response to sexual assault cases. Those agencies with their responsibilities and roles are as follows:
Key Partners:
1. Domestic Violence Shelters: Alice’s Place and White Mountain Safe House offer safe, culturally sensitive support to domestic violence victims,  
emphasizing advocacy, shelter, education, and resources.
2. ChangePoint Integrated Health: Our county's counseling center collaborates with us by attending SART meetings, providing mental health  
therapy services to crime victims, and assisting in outreach and public awareness events. They also oversee the White Mountain Safehouse.
3. Law Enforcement Agencies: Committed to providing a safe environment, they support the entire county, including unincorporated areas. Some  
officers are trained in forensic interviewing for sex crime cases.
• Navajo County Sheriff’s Department
• Holbrook Police Department
• Winslow Police Department
• Snowflake-Taylor Police Department
• Show Low Police Department
• Pinetop/Lakeside Department
4. Navajo County Family Advocacy Center (FAC): A non-profit arm of the Navajo County Attorney’s Office, they provide forensic interviews and  
victim services at centers in opposite sides of our county, Holbrook and Show Low. The Show Low center offers Sexual Assault Nurse Exams  
(SANE) in partnership with Summit Integrated Healthcare for victims aged 18 and younger.
5. Northern Arizona Care and Services After Assault (NACASA): They offer SANE exams for sexual assault victims aged 13 and up in Flagstaff and  
Show Low. Their close collaboration with our SART includes participation in multiple programs, outreach, and education initiatives.
6. Navajo County Sexual Assault Response Team (SART) Coordinator: Managed by the Navajo County Victim Services Department, this  
coordinator has close access to county prosecutors and advocates. This partnership ensures the protection of victims' rights and active participation  
in SART team meetings, investigations, and protocol development.
7. Navajo County Victim Services Department: The only Victim Services Program located outside Tribal Land in Navajo County, they provide 24/7  
crisis response advocacy, criminal justice support, and victim compensation services. Their reach extends county-wide, including Superior Court,  
local Justice Courts, Juvenile Court, and post-conviction hearings. Additionally, they operate a 24/7 Crisis Response Team and collaborate with the  
Navajo County Family Advocacy Center. Their crisis responders, manager, and victim compensation coordinator are actively involved in our SART  
program.

agencies contract with the Department of Child Services.  She has experience working with a multi-disciplinary taskforce.  Her experience is directly

this project and be responsible for implementing the action plan created for the SART program.
The Victim Services Manager supervises the SART Coordinator. The victim services manager has been employed with the County Attorney’s Office  
for 14 years. She has been the manager of victim services for 10 years. She is a certified advocate and has specialized training and experience in  
serving victims of sexual assault. She has experience with developing multi-disciplinary teams (MDT) as she assisted with the development of our  
local child abuse MDT and presently manages the MDT Coordinator.  Several agencies who participate in our MDT are also SART partners. She  
has extensive experience with the development and implementation of public awareness events, training, and outreach. Every year during victim’s  
rights week, she manages a team that hosts a Victims Rights Symposium in Navajo County that produces free, accredited local training for the

Office for 10 years and was previously the Communications Director the Navajo County Administration. She has a degree in Business and  
Management, extensive experience in providing fiscal management for an organization and writing and maintaining grants. The Office Manager  
manages grants and maintains the $8.5M budget and manages 8 grants for the County Attorney’s Office. She will spend 10% of her time on this  
program. She will report on financial and programmatic activities required for the grant. She will provide support and guidance to the program as  
needed, and ensure the program is meeting the Grants requirements.
The Office Manager and the Victim Services Manager report directly to the Elected County Attorney who has been in his position for 15 years. Since

Capacity Building – A SART’s strength is directly related to the professional relationships that it builds and maintains. Strengthening existing

time will be focused on continuing to maintain and strengthen our professional relationships with all our current SART agencies; Law Enforcement,

SART meetings. It is important that the staff at these agencies are in a position to provide services to sex crime victims, are educated on our County  
Protocol, are knowledgeable about the dynamics of sexual assault, and have the skill set to best work with victims in the scope of the job they  
perform. In addition to strengthening existing relationships, our SART Coordinator will identify, through data tracking with partner agencies gaps in  
services. The SART Coordinator will glean data through case review and will then coordinate protocol review and maintenance as needed. For the

Coordinator will perform outreach to the medical community including the Indian Health Hospitals. Our Coordinator will also continue to build  
partnerships with existing SART programs throughout the State and utilize them for support and education.
Fiscally Administered Grants – Grants are written, internally approved prior to submission, and then approved by the County Board of Supervisors.  
Expenses are approved by the Office Manager and then reviewed on the fund detailed general ledger (DGL). Salary and ERE expenses are  
processed through a timesheet/payroll process and then reviewed on the DGL. Financial reports are created by the Office Manager with an internal  
audit completed by a Finance Department team member prior to submission for reimbursement. A fiscal year-end review with the Financial  
Department is conducted to ensure funds were reported properly.
Sustaining Programs - Currently, the County Attorney’s Office has Victim Service grants through ACJC’s Victims’ Compensation Fund, DPS VOCA  
and the AG’s Office. We also utilize funds from General Fund, fees from Diversions, the Criminal Justice Enhancement Fund, and ACJS’s Fill-the-
Gap funds. We are constantly exploring diversified funding opportunities to strengthen our financial capacity to provide services to victims of crime.

10. Evaluation Plan (100 points)
Program Evaluation (1500 word limit)
Evaluation Plan
Monitoring Performance – The SART Coordinator will gather and report the progress of the Navajo County SART program. The Victim Services  
Manager and the SART Coordinator will be overall responsible for monitoring performance measures for our SART program and ensuring our  
program is satisfying our goals in line with our strategic plan and funder’s requirements. Additional oversight is provided by the Office Manager,  
responsible for managing the grant.
Resources - Our program will require funds to employ our SART Coordinator. The SART Coordinator is responsible for coordinating program  
outputs, monitoring progress and evaluating the effectiveness of the program. Outreach supplies, training supplies, training-related travel, data  
collection tools are the resources needed for the program. These resources are outlined in the budget detail and narrative but are also listed as  
follows: Salary and ERE for SART Coordinator, office supplies to maintain SART materials, and funds for printing costs for our fliers and brochures.  
We will need travel, hotel, and food funds for our SART Coordinator and Victim Services manager to travel within the State, as well as attend a  
national conference.  
Collecting/Analyzing Data - Our SART Coordinator will utilize multiple tools to evaluate our programs progress towards meeting our goals.
• Case tracking- The SART Coordinator is the nucleus of our county’s response to sex crime victims.  She will track sexual crime cases through  
referrals from our SART, crisis intake forms by victim services department, and obtaining case information as they are referred to the County  
Attorney’s Office.  She will reach out monthly to collect sex crime information from our law enforcement partners to identify cases that were not  
served by our SART to use for evaluation purposes.  The Coordinator is central to the triage of services, and is relied upon as the expert to help  
agencies navigate and information share.  SART protocol dictates when any SART member agency comes into contact with a victim of sexual  
assault, they are required to notify a victim advocate to provide assistance to that victim. Each victim’s case will be tracked using an internal,  
confidential, tracking spreadsheet. The SART Coordinator will track the services provided, case investigation, prosecution and outcomes using this  
spreadsheet. Our case tracking information will include both statistical data, and anecdotal data to aid in case review for each victim. Cases will be  
reviewed monthly at SART meetings.
• We utilize victim surveys through Survey Monkey to monitor the effectiveness of our program’s coordinated response. The purpose of the survey is  
to measure the effectiveness of the victim-centered services received. The SART coordinator will follow up with victims annually to survey them on  
the SART’s effectiveness. This data will be reviewed quarterly and annually.
• We will also use Survey Monkey to survey our partners on SART. Surveys will be administered each year in September. The SART Coordinator  
will receive feedback on how our program is currently performing and will then modify the program model accordingly.  
• We will utilize the Outcomes for Human Trafficking Survivors Instrument, recommended by the National Institute for Justice to learn and evaluate  
our effectiveness as we enhance our support to sex trafficking victims. In addition, we will study and utilize the data provided by the Arizona Human  
Trafficking Council.
• We will track our outreach activity on an internal outreach tracking spreadsheet on Microsoft excel for program reporting. This data will be reviewed
through monthly expense tracking.
• On-Board Training effectiveness will be measured through a training survey conducted at the end of each training session. Number of trainings  
conducted will be stored for program reporting. Surveys will be conducted at time of training.  Training will be evaluated once a year through our  
partner survey.  
Organizing Data - Our data will be organized using spreadsheets, current data tracking software, financial expenditures tracking through the Detailed
General Ledger, timesheets, and survey results. All data and information received by SART Coordinator will be redacted to not include any  
identifying information for a victim. This information is stored on our County secure servers.
Analyzing and Utilizing Data – Expenses will be reviewed and analyzed monthly to determine the month-to-date expenditures are aligned with the  
budget. Victim assistance will be measured, collected and analyzed through surveys collected. The effectiveness of the outreach activities can be  
measured through increased referrals from the medical communities, as we expect to see an increase in referrals. For our year one data collecting  
measures for the study of human trafficking as well as case flow process between FAC victims and prosecution referral, data will be tabulated and  
recorded for assessment in year 2.  When completing quarterly programmatic reports, the Office Manager, Victim Services Manager and the SART  
Coordinator will review data. Changes resulting from the data will be implemented into the program to ensure program progress can be achieved.
Program Improvements – Data will be reviewed quarterly and annually to identify and compare results. A year over year data review can identify  
commonalities that both positively and negatively impacts a victim’s access to resources and our ability to successfully prosecute their case. This  
feedback will be shared with the SART. If necessary, protocols and policies will be updated to identify and fill any gaps in services.  We are anxious  
to get our hands on the data we will track for human trafficking and case flow process for FAC victims.

Maintenance and Radiation Survey. Annual Preventive Maintenance and Radiation Survey:
“Preventive Maintenance” consists of performing fundamental planned maintenance
activity, with the goal of improving equipment life by preventing excess depreciation and
impairment. At the time of scheduling Preventive Maintenance, the Customer may request
Operator Refresher Training and Daily Inspection Procedures training. The frequency of the
Preventive Maintenance, Radiation Survey and Training visits shall occur annually. There is
no limitation to the number of claims per year, excluding repairs needed due to misuse or
abuse. Technical Telephone Support: “Telephone Support” consists of responding to
telephone and e-mail inquiries received by the Astrophysics Service Department regarding
equipment errors. During regular business hours, the Astrophysics Service Department will
respond to the Customer within two (2) hours from initial contact. Additional support is

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. t.        
Meeting Date: 02/27/2024  
Title: NCSO Tahoe Purchase Revision
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff 
Submitted By: Kimberley Willis, Sheriff's Office Finance Manager
Department: Sheriff 
Motion before the Board:
Revision of a previously approved agenda item for the purchase of 10 Tahoes
Background:
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office was approved for the purchase of 10 Tahoes in the amount of
$568,703.20 from Courtesy Chevrolet on November 14, 2023, by the Board of Supervisors.  This
purchase was part of NCSO's FY24 fleet replacement/maintenance approved budget. Due to 
circumstances outside NCSO's control, the Tahoes were not secured by the vendor and as a result, the
order was modified. Courtesy Chevrolet was able to substitute nine (9) 2024 Chevrolet 1500 Crew Cab
pickups for a total of $485,230.86. Additionally, NCSO was able to locate a Tahoe from a local dealer,
Horne Auto Center, in the amount of $72,235.71.  The grand total of the ten (10) vehicles is $557,466.57,
being less than the original approve purchase amount.
The Office is requesting consideration and approval on the revised vehicle purchase(s) to include:
substitution of nine (9) 2024 Chevrolet pickups and one (1) Chevrolet Tahoe for the originally approved
ten (10) tahoes; and an additional vendor, being Horne Auto Center.  Courtesy Chevrolet is a state
contracted vendor, and 3 quotes were obtained for the Hone Auto Center purchase, as per the Navajo
County procurement policy.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. u.        
Meeting Date: 02/27/2024  
Title: Arizona Criminal Justice and Treatment Improvement Program Grant Agreement
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff 
Submitted By: Kimberley Willis, Sheriff's Office Finance Manager
Department: Sheriff 
Motion before the Board:
Grant agreement between the Arizona Criminal Justice Commission and the Navajo County Sheriff's
Office in the amount of $350,000 
Background:
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office was awarded grant funding from the Department of Justice, Office of
Justice Programs, through the Arizona Criminal Justice Commission as a part of the Comprehensive
Opioid, Stimulant, and Substance Abuse Program (COSSAP). This project was developed as part of the
Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) legislation with the purpose of providing financial
and technical assistance for the development and implementation efforts in identifying, responding,
treating, and supporting those impacted by illicit opioids, stimulants, and other drugs of abuse. Funding
awarded in the amount of $350,000 includes salary and ERE for a Special Programs Manager, $247,500
for contractual services with YouTurn Health, and $7,500 for other operating expenses. 
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office is preparing to implement a program at its detention facility to aid in
the successful re-entry of detainees into society. This program will encourage users to overcome
addiction, return to society as self-sufficient and responsible residents, and promote community
partnerships addressing violent crimes, illicit drug use, and recidivism in our communities. The Special
Programs Manager will coordinate efforts with organizations who specialize in providing the most
successful re-entry options upon release from custody, as well as seeking additional funding sources for
the continued operation of the program. Additionally, NCSO will be contracting with YouTurn Health,
which offers Peer Recovery Support Services (PRSS) virtually by providing education and support for
incarcerated subjects struggling with mental health, substance misuse, or suicidal ideation. 
This agreement will commence on January 1, 2024, and terminate on December 31, 2024.

For each individual at least 18 years of age who is a covered individual under this FY 2019

Steps to sign a DocuSign Document  
DocuSign is an electronic document service that allows parties to an agreement to review a 
document and apply an e-signature to that document. DocuSign is a safe and secure way to 
electronically send and sign documents. You do not need the DocuSign service to sign a 
document. Please check your "JUNK MAIL" to ensure that the DocuSign email was received.  
ACJC will send you a DocuSign email containing a link to your document.  
Review the DocuSign email: Open the email and review the message from the sender. C lick 
REVIEW DOCUMENT to begin the signing process.  
Agree to sign electronically: Review the consumer disclosure, and select the checkbox I agree 
to use Electronic Records and Signatures.  
Important! To view and sign the documents, you must agree to conduct business electronically.  
Note: To view additional options, click the OTHER ACTIONS button on the right side of the 
page. Other Actions are options such as Decline to Sign if you want to decline to sign the 
document or Assign to Someone Else if you are not the appropriate person to sign the 
document.  
Click CONTINUE to begin the signing process.  
Start the signing process:  
Click the START tag on the left to begin the signing process. You are taken to the first tag 
requiring your action.  
Click the SIGN tag. If this is the first time you are using DocuSign, You are asked to 
Adopt Your Signature.  
 
To Adopt your initials and signature:  
To adopt your initials and signature, verify that your name and initials are correct. If not, change 
them as needed. Click on Choose Change Style to see a variety of signature and initial styles. 
You can also choose to draw your signature and initials or upload a signature and initials.  
Once you have selected your choice, Click ADOPT AND SIGN to adopt and save your 
signature information and return to the document.  
Sign the document: 
 After reviewing the document, you are now ready to sign the document. Click on all of the 
signature tags to place your initials or signature on the document. If you miss one and try to 
DocuSign Envelope ID: F105FAFB-312A-4FB4-AF66-5B0AA239E5BE

<!-- page 651 -->
submit it, you will be routed to the tags that still require a signature or initials.  
For any red boxes in the document, type in the relevant information, such as your title.  
Confirm signing:  
When you finish clicking all signature tags in the document, confirm signing by clicking FINISH. 
A message appears stating that you have completed your document. You can now download a 
PDF copy or print a copy of the document. The sender receives an email with the signed 
document attached, and the signed document appears in their DocuSign account.  
Sign up for a DocuSign account: 
After signing the document and clicking the Finish button, you will get a message offering to Sign 
up for a DocuSign account and save the document in your account. You do not need to sign up 
for an account. A DocuSign account allows you to save all documents in an account. Keep in 
mind that after all parties have signed the document you will receive a pdf copy of the agreement. 
If you do not desire a DocuSign account, just choose No Thanks.  
Finish 
This completes the process of  signing a DocuSign document. If you have any questions, 
concerns, or problems with the DocuSign e-signature process, please contact your ACJC grant 
coordinator at scourter@azcjc.gov for clarification.

ELECTRONIC RECORD AND SIGNATURE DISCLOSURE  
From time to time, Arizona Criminal Justice Commission (we, us or Company) may be required 
by law to provide to you certain written notices or disclosures. Described below are the terms 
and conditions for providing to you such notices and disclosures electronically through the 
DocuSign system. Please read the information below carefully and thoroughly, and if you can 
access this information electronically to your satisfaction and agree to this Electronic Record and 
Signature Disclosure (ERSD), please confirm your agreement by selecting the check-box next to 
‘I agree to use electronic records and signatures’ before clicking ‘CONTINUE’ within the 
DocuSign system. 
 
Getting paper copies  
At any time, you may request from us a paper copy of any record provided or made available 
electronically to you by us. You will have the ability to download and print documents we send 
to you through the DocuSign system during and immediately after the signing session and, if you 
elect to create a DocuSign account, you may access the documents for a limited period of time 
(usually 30 days) after such documents are first sent to you. After such time, if you wish for us to 
send you paper copies of any such documents from our office to you, you will be charged a 
$0.00 per-page fee. You may request delivery of such paper copies from us by following the 
procedure described below. 
 
Withdrawing your consent  
If you decide to receive notices and disclosures from us electronically, you may at any time 
change your mind and tell us that thereafter you want to receive required notices and disclosures 
only in paper format. How you must inform us of your decision to receive future notices and 
disclosure in paper format and withdraw your consent to receive notices and disclosures 
electronically is described below. 
 
Consequences of changing your mind  
If you elect to receive required notices and disclosures only in paper format, it will slow the 
speed at which we can complete certain steps in transactions with you and delivering services to 
you because we will need first to send the required notices or disclosures to you in paper format, 
and then wait until we receive back from you your acknowledgment of your receipt of such 
paper notices or disclosures. Further, you will no longer be able to use the DocuSign system to 
receive required notices and consents electronically from us or to sign electronically documents 
from us. 
 
All notices and disclosures will be sent to you electronically

inadvertently not receiving any notice or disclosure, we prefer to provide all of the required 
notices and disclosures to you by the same method and to the same address that you have given 
us. Thus, you can receive all the disclosures and notices electronically or in paper format through 
the paper mail delivery system. If you do not agree with this process, please let us know as 
described below. Please also see the paragraph immediately above that describes the 
consequences of your electing not to receive delivery of the notices and disclosures 
electronically from us. 
 
How to contact Arizona Criminal Justice Commission:  
You may contact us to let us know of your changes as to how we may contact you electronically, 
to request paper copies of certain information from us, and to withdraw your prior consent to 
receive notices and disclosures electronically as follows: 
To contact us by email send messages to: alefevre@azcjc.gov 
 
To advise Arizona Criminal Justice Commission of your new email address  
To let us know of a change in your email address where we should send notices and disclosures 
electronically to you, you must send an email message to us at alefevre@azcjc.gov and in the 
body of such request you must state: your previous email address, your new email address.  We 
do not require any other information from you to change your email address.  
If you created a DocuSign account, you may update it with your new email address through your 
account preferences.  
 
To request paper copies from Arizona Criminal Justice Commission  
To request delivery from us of paper copies of the notices and disclosures previously provided 
by us to you electronically, you must send us an email to alefevre@azcjc.gov and in the body of 
such request you must state your email address, full name, mailing address, and telephone 
number. We will bill you for any fees at that time, if any. 
 
To withdraw your consent with Arizona Criminal Justice Commission  
To inform us that you no longer wish to receive future notices and disclosures in electronic 
format you may:

Title: United States Geological Survey Stream Monitoring Joint Funding Agreement
Submitted For: William Flake, Assistant County Engineer 
Submitted By: Julianna Davis, Hydrologly Technician 
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Joint Funding Agreement with the United States Geological Survey (USGS) for the period of October 1,
2023, to September 30, 2026, for operating and maintaining seven (7) surface water gauging stations
Background:
Navajo County Department of Public Works has teamed with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) over
many years to operate and maintain surface water gauging stations. We have attached the state map
showing where our seven (7) gauges are located. This partnership is important in having data collected
and stored by another responsible entity that documents the flows in the main rivers and contributing
tributaries in the County, and contributes to important mutually beneficial water resources studies.

THIS AGREEMENT is entered into as of the October 1, 2023, by the U.S. GEOLOGICAL SURVEY, Arizona Water 
Science Center, UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, party of the first part, and the Navajo County 
Public Works Department party of the second part. 
1. The parties hereto agree that subject to the availability of appropriations and in accordance with their respective
authorities there shall be maintained in cooperation Water Resource Investigations (per attachment), herein called
the program. The USGS legal authority is 43 USC 36C; 43 USC 50, and 43 USC 50b.
2. The following amounts shall be contributed to cover all of the cost of the necessary field and analytical work
directly related to this program. 2(b) include In-Kind-Services in the amount of $0.00.
(a) $137,400 by the party of t he first part during the period 
October 1, 2023 to September 30, 2026 
(b) $209,100 by the party of t he second part during the period 
October 1, 2023 to September 30, 2026 
(c) Contributions are provided by the party of the firs t part through other USGS regional or national programs,
in the amount of: $62,100
Description of the USGS regional/national program: USGS Federal Priority Stream Gage Network
(d) Additional or reduced amounts by each party durin g the above period or succeeding periods as may be
determined by mutual agreement and set forth in an exchange of letters between the parties.
(e) The performance period may be changed by mutual agreement and set forth in an exchange of letters
between the parties.
3. The costs of this program may be paid by either party in conformity with the laws and regulations respectively
governing each party.
4. The field and analytical work pertaining to this program shall be under the direction of or subject to periodic review
by an authorized representative of the party of the first part.
5. The areas to be included in the program shall be determined by mutual agreement between the parties hereto or
their authorized representatives. The methods employed in the field and office shall be those adopted by the party of
the first part to insure the required standards of accuracy subject to modification by mutual agreement.
6. During the course of this program, all field and analytical work of either party pertaining to this program shall be
open to the inspection of the other party, and if the work is not being carried on in a mutually satisfactory manner,
either party may terminate this agreement upon 60 days written notice to the other party.
7. The original records resulting from this program will be deposited in the office of origin of those records. Upon
request, copies of the original records will be provided to the office of the other party.
8. The maps, records or reports resulting from this program shall be made available to the public as promptly as
possible. The maps, records or reports normally will be published by the party of the first part. However, the party of
the second part reserves the right to publish the results of this program, and if already published by the party of the
first part shall, upon request, be furnished by the party of the first part, at cost, impressions suitable for purposes of
reproduction similar to that for which the original copy was prepared. The maps, records or reports published by
either party shall contain a statement of the cooperative relations between the parties. The Parties acknowledge that
scientific information and data developed as a result of the Scope of Work (SOW) are subject to applicable USGS
review, approval, and release requirements, which are available on the USGS Fundamental Science Practices
website (https://www2.usgs.gov/fsp/).

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. w.        
Meeting Date: 02/27/2024  
Title: Funding Agreement with Arizona Department of Housing on Community Development
Block Grant
Submitted By: Kenichi Maruyama, Strategic Initiatives Manager
Department: Administrative Services Division: Finance
Motion before the Board:
Agreement between the Arizona Department of Housing and Navajo County to receive $131,000 from
FY2023 Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Program for Pinetop-Lakeside Senior Citizens
Inc Community Center Improvements Project and make a non-profit funding agreement with the Senior
Citizens Inc to administer the project in compliance with CDBG regulations 
Background:
Navajo County administers 2023 Community Development Block Grant (CDGB) Program. In January
2023, the County Board of Supervisors approved roof replacement of Clay Springs Community Center
for use of the County's CDBG funds. 
Arizona Department of Housing (ADOH) serves as a pass-through agency by receiving CDBG funds
from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and distributing the funds to rural
communities in the state. Northern Arizona Council of Governments (NACOG) oversees the planning of
annual allocations and provides technical assistance for application as well as project success in our
region. 
ADOH also requires a funding agreement between the County and Pinetop-Lakeside Senior Citizens, Inc.
Upon execution of these funding agreements, the County and the Senior Citizens, Inc. collaborate to
administer a grant in compliance with the terms and conditions. Designated staff will be authorized to sign
administrative documents related to the grant and sign payment requests related to the grant. Then, the
County will receive reimbursement payments from ADOH. 
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: 2024
Budgeted Y/N:
Amount Requested:
Fiscal Impact:
The project will get funded 100% from the grant. No local match is required.

Section 11.   ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW CONDITIONS 
 
In accordance with 24 CFR 50 and 24 CF R 58 ( “Environmental Review ”), the 
environmental effects of each activity carried out with federal funds must be assessed.  Local 
government entities are responsible for conducting environmental reviews and requesting a 
release of funds from ADOH.  Non -profits and other non -governmental entities are 
responsible for conducting Environmental Reviews before ADOH requests a release of funds 
from HUD.  Completion of the Environmental Revi ew Record (“ERR”) is mandatory before 
taking any physical action on a site or entering into contracts.  Only exempt activities such as 
architecture, engineering and administration may be undertaken and reimbursed by ADOH 
prior to receiving a written release of funds.  Exempt activities described in 24 CFR 58.34(a)(1)-
(11) are activities that generally have no physical impact on the environment.  If federal funds 
are involved in a project, neither federal nor non -federal funds may be expended or 
committed by contract (conditional or not) for property acquisition, rehabilitation,

<!-- page 680 -->
Funding Agreement with 
State of Arizona, Department of Housing  
REV. 6/14/2023 12 
conversion, lease, repair or construction activities, until HUD or ADOH has provided written 
authorization based on approval of an ERR.  
 
 An option agreement (to purchase land) on a proposed site or property is allowable 
prior to the completion of the E nvironmental Review if the option agreement is contingent 
upon an ADOH or HUD authorization to use funds based on a completed ERR.  The cost of 
the option must be a nominal portion of the purchase price.  
 
Projects funded solely with Housing Trust Funds do not require an ERR but are 
required to meet the requirements of the State Historic Preservation Act by consulting with 
the State Historic Pr eservation Office (SHPO).  For State Housing Funded projects , Phase I 
Environmental Assessments are required to be completed on properties for which new 
construction/change in use is proposed, regardless of whether federal or state funds are the 
source of funding.  Expenditures incurred or obligated by construction contract prior to 
ADOH’s release of funds or consultation with SHPO will not be reimbursed by ADOH.   
  
 Recipients who had committed or expended non -federal funds to begin a project 
before receiving the authorization from ADOH or HUD may still be eligible to use federal 
funds on the project under the following circumstances:  
 
(a) Recipients started the project without the intention of using f ederal assistance 
(i.e. as evidenced by other anticipated funding, the original project budget, etc.); 
 
(b) All work on the project ceases once an application for federal funds is made and 
an ERR is begun on all activities  (i.e. acquisition, construction, etc.).  ADOH or 
HUD provides authorization to proceed based on the completed ERR.  
 
 WEATHERIZATION (DOE WAP, DOE WAP BIL, DOE WRF, LIHEAP WAP).  DOE 
has made a final NEPA determination for all activities under this Funding Agreement 
that are listed in the State Plan formally approved by DOE and incorporated into this 
Funding Agreement.  Recipients are responsible for compliance with Section 106

Subject to availability of and receipt of funds from th e State’s Unclaimed Property

Recipient may request funds only after the date of the executed Agreement and other

applicable federal rules and regulations, including requirements by the Federal Office of

Recipient’s right to incur expenses under this Agreement shall cease upon expiration
